objective.statement: Name and write intervals on a stave that has a key signature.
successCriteria: I work out what each note really is before I name the interval.
I know a written natural, sharp or flat overrides the key signature for that note.
I add a sign to a note I write only when the key signature does not already give it.

explanation.text: When a stave has a key signature, it changes every note of those letters, in every octave, unless a sign in front of a note says otherwise. So before you name an interval, work out what each note is: first the key signature, then any sign written in front of the note. The name of an interval depends only on the two notes themselves, not on the key signature they happen to be written in.

music.textAlternative: In D major, F sharp then A.

explanation.caption: D major (F♯ and C♯): the first note is F♯, so F♯ up to A is a minor 3rd. F up to A with no signature would be a major 3rd.

explanation.text: A sign in front of a note beats the key signature for that note, and a sign always means exactly what it says. In G major the signature gives F♯, but a natural sign makes that note F♮: B up to F♮ is a diminished 5th, where B up to F♯ would be a perfect 5th. A sign can also go on a letter the signature leaves alone, in either direction, even in a sharp key: in D major a flat sign gives A♭, not A♮.

music.textAlternative: In G major, B then F natural, written with a natural sign.

explanation.caption: G major: the natural sign cancels the signature's F♯, so this is B up to F♮, a diminished 5th.

music.textAlternative: In D major, C natural then A flat, each written with its own sign.

explanation.caption: D major (F♯ and C♯): the natural sign cancels the signature's C♯, and the flat sign gives A♭ even though the key is a sharp key. C♮ up to A♭ is a minor 6th.

explanation.text: Writing an interval works the same way, in reverse. Find the letter by counting, then the accidental the quality needs, and compare that with what the key signature already gives the letter. If they match, write no sign. If they differ, write the sign. A minor 3rd above E♭ is G♭; in A♭ major the signature has no flat on G, so the G♭ needs a flat sign. A major 3rd above E♭ is G♮, and it needs no sign. Signature first, then any sign in front of the note, then count letters and check the quality.

guided.prompt: The key signature shows 2 sharps (B minor). Name the interval between these two notes, from the lower to the higher: give its quality and its number. Remember that the key signature applies to every note on the stave.

music.textAlternative: A treble-clef stave, key signature of 2 sharps. a note in the 1st space; a note in the 2nd space.

hints: Work out what each note really is (signature, then any sign in front of it), then count letters for the number and compare with the major scale of the lower note for the quality.

First work out what each note really is: the key signature changes every note of that letter unless a sign in front of the note cancels it or changes it again. Then count the letter names for the number and compare with the major scale of the lower note for the quality.

feedback.correct: Yes: the key signature first, then the interval.

mistakes.counted-one-end-only: Count both the lower and the upper note.
mistakes.quality-from-wrong-key: Compare the upper note with the major scale of the LOWER note.
mistakes.compound-arithmetic: An octave plus a 5th is a 12th, not a 13th: the shared note is counted only once.
mistakes.enharmonic-spelling: The letter names decide the number, even when two spellings sound alike.
mistakes.augmented-diminished-swap: Larger by a semitone: diminished, minor, major, augmented.
mistakes.ignored-key-signature: The key signature changes every note of its letters unless a sign in front of the note says otherwise: work out each note first.

feedback.fallback: Not quite. Count the letter names first, then compare with the major scale on the lower note.
